notes: liber, libri, m.: the stem is libr-, so there is no e after the nominative; the noun is a homograph of the adjective liber, libera, liberum (free)
annus: the ablative plural annis carries the length of a life here, where classical Latin would use the accusative of duration
filia, filiæ, f.: dative and ablative plural filiabus, to keep it apart from filiis of filius
ortus, ortus, m.: fourth declension, built on the supine stem of orior
generatio: genitive plural generationum
similitudo: genitive plural similitudinum
imago: genitive plural imaginum
tempus: genitive plural temporum, neuter plural tempora
opus: genitive plural operum, neuter plural opera
labor: genitive plural laborum
dies is feminine in 5:1 (in die qua) and masculine in 5:2 (in die quo) — one noun, two genders, and the relative pronoun beside it is the only thing that shows which
Mathusala, Mathusalæ, m.: first declension but masculine, with the accusative Mathusalam (5:21, 5:22); the genitive in 5:27 is left uninflected as Mathusala, not Mathusalæ
Cainan, Malaleel, Jared, Noë, Sem, Cham and Japheth are indeclinable, as are Adam, Seth, Enos, Henoch and Lamech; only the context gives their case
Noë keeps its diæresis in every form and never adds an ending
centum, triginta, quadraginta, sexaginta, septuaginta, octoginta, nonaginta, quinque, septem, novem, decem, duodecim and quindecim are all indeclinable
trecenti, quingenti, septingenti, octingenti and nongenti decline like the plural of bonus and have no singular at all
duo, duæ, duo: declines like nothing else in the language, and its ablative duobus is one of only three forms it has
the numbers here are simply set side by side with no et between them (centum triginta annis), so each numeral agrees with the noun on its own
vivo, vivere, vixi, victus: the supine victus is shared with vinco (to conquer) and is rare from vivo
gigno, gignere, genui, genitus: the present is reduplicated from the root gen-, which the perfect and supine show plain
morior, mori, mortuus sum: deponent, and its perfect participle mortuus stands as the adjective 'dead' as well
consolor, consolari, consolatus sum: deponent, and it takes ab with the ablative for what it consoles you from
appareo, apparere, apparui, apparitus: the supine is rare, and the perfect apparui has no v
fio, fieri, factus sum: passive in form, active in meaning, and its perfect is written as two words (facti sunt)
fero, ferre, tuli, latus: three unrelated stems for one verb — fer-, tul-, lat-
maledico, maledicere, maledixi, maledictus: a compound of dico governing the dative (cui maledixit), so the imperative is maledic, not maledice

cum is a preposition here (cum Deo, 5:22 and 5:24) and a conjunction in 5:31 (cum esset): one surface form, two words, so the preposition is cited 'cum (preposition)' to keep the two dictionary entries apart
postquam takes the indicative, unlike cum, which takes the subjunctive in this chapter
noster, nostra, nostrum: the stem is nostr-, so there is no e in nostri or nostrarum
quingentorum esset annorum in 5:31 is a genitive of description — 'was of five hundred years' — where English says 'was five hundred years old'
